units: a shopkeeper looks back on her early days at a wholesale market
at the start she had bought too many perishable goods
unsold crates piled up behind her stall
an experienced middleman suggested she split her orders
he told her to watch the buyers before purchasing anything
she wrote down in a notebook the requests she could not meet
she started her trade again with a narrower range
her profit doubled without her selling space changing
text: The woman who ran the counter talked me through her first season at the wholesale market. She had bought far too much soft fruit at the start, she said, certain that the buyers would follow. The crates nobody wanted stacked up behind the stall, and by evening the smell of ripe pulp caught in her throat. An older broker told her to cut every order in half and to spend her mornings watching the aisles before committing to anything at all. She kept to that for a whole season. In a cloth notebook she wrote down what shoppers asked for and could not find, and what they walked past even when the price was low. When winter came she opened again with a shorter list of goods, chosen this time. Her margin had doubled, she added with a smile, and the stall had not grown by a single shelf.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: better roads transformed the economy of the countryside
poor harvests once caused local shortages that could not be filled
heavy wagons became able to travel even in the bad season
the surplus of one region made up for what another lacked
the price of grain stopped varying sharply from place to place
growers began to raise a single crop
they kept the crop that paid them the most
the hands thus freed were taken on by the workshops of the market towns
text: Better cart roads reshaped the rural economy far more deeply than the men who had paid for them ever expected. As long as harvests moved along muddy tracks, every farming basin had to feed itself, and a failed harvest left behind a shortage that nothing from outside could fill. Once heavy wagons could roll through the wet months, the surplus of one valley made up for what the next one lacked, and the price of grain stopped swinging violently from district to district. That steadiness brought a result nobody had planned for. The growers narrowed their fields down to a single crop, dropping the side plantings and keeping whatever paid them best. The hands that this narrowing set free drifted down to the market towns, where the workshops took them on without the least trouble.

units: a workshop can hold orders and still lack ready money
suppliers and staff are paid before the customers pay
an invoice sent out is a sum owed but not received
payment often arrives after the spending has already happened
financial health depends on the pace at which money comes in
asking for a payment up front brings funds in early
steady reminders sent before the due date help payment along
a body can advance the money and take on recovering the sums
text: A small workshop can hold a full order book and still run out of money by the following week. The whole trouble lies in the timing of it. It pays its suppliers and its staff long before its customers pay it. Every invoice it sends out is money owed but not yet in hand, and the day it falls due sits well past the day the costs were met. Financial health, then, rests less on profit than on the pace at which cash comes in. Three remedies are open to a workshop in that position. The first is to ask for a payment up front when the order is placed, which brings funds in from the outset. The second is to send steady, courteous reminders ahead of the agreed date. The third costs more: hand the unpaid invoices to a body that advances the money and takes over the work of collecting it.

units: two workshops in the same trade stood on the same street
the first kept about ten workers and took every order
the second was run by a couple who turned down ordinary work
the larger workshop coped badly with the slack periods
its fixed costs ran on while its machines stood idle
the couple came through those periods with no financial harm
when demand returned the big workshop raised its output fast
the couple could then take on no extra order
each of the two approaches won in one season and lost in the other
text: Two binding workshops stood on the same street, only a few doors apart, and lived off the same trade. The first kept about ten workers on the floor and took every order that came through the door, however plain the work. The second belonged to a married couple who turned away any job that called for neither gilding nor chosen leather. Through the slack months the larger shop struggled, since its fixed costs ran on while its presses stood idle. The couple crossed the same weeks unharmed, because what they spent went on materials and on their own labor. When demand picked up, the picture flipped. One of them doubled its output inside a week. The other hit a ceiling and had to turn away the extra work. Each of the two ways of trading won in one season what it gave back in the next.

units: it is wise to read an employment contract before signing it
the section on hours may hold a duty to stay reachable
you must ask what pay is set for those periods of availability
the bonus announced may be guaranteed or left to the manager's choice
the length of the trial period and the terms of ending it are worth checking
a mobility clause forces a change of site if the employer decides so
you may ask for a copy of the document and take it home
an employer who pushes the candidate to sign gives away some flaw
text: Before you sign an employment contract, put the pen back down and read it slowly. Start with the section on hours. That is where on-call time tends to hide, meaning stretches when you have to stay reachable without being at work. Ask straight out how those hours are going to be paid, and have the answer written into the document. Move on to pay, and find out whether the bonus you were promised is owed to you or left to your manager's say-so. After that, look at the trial period, how long it runs and how either side can end it. Then check the mobility clause, which ties you to moving sites whenever the company decides. If something is unclear, ask for a copy and take it home. A sound employer will not mind. One who pushes you to sign on the spot is telling you plenty already.

units: a stoppage began early outside a logistics warehouse
the night shift staff broke off their work first
machine drivers and truck drivers joined them before midday
the strikers want a frozen bonus scale reopened
they demand the scrapping of a computer program that tracks every movement
management refused at first to talk under pressure
a delegation was received in the evening with no result
the vehicles were sent on to two nearby depots
deliveries to neighborhood shops ran late
the dispute is spreading to another site of the same company
text: The walkout began at first light outside the gates of a logistics warehouse. The night-shift sorters dropped their work first, and by late morning the forklift drivers and a part of the truck crews had joined them. They want a bonus scale that has been frozen for three seasons reopened, and they want the firm to drop a pacing program that, they say, tracks every movement a worker makes. Management said at the outset that it would not bargain under pressure, then agreed to see a delegation early in the evening. That meeting produced nothing whatsoever. Stranded trucks were rerouted to two nearby depots, which held up deliveries to the neighborhood shops. A mediator is due to take the talks up again tomorrow, while the action spreads to a second site belonging to the same firm.

units: a smell of grain reaches you before you enter the building
the stacked sacks give off a heat that raises a haze
the lack of ventilation forces the doors open very early
birds come in through those openings and cannot be driven away
constant use has hollowed out the pans of the scales
the passing of carts has cracked the brick floor
the jolting spills what is inside the badly tied sacks
the workers give up sweeping because the dirt comes back quickly
text: You catch the smell of grain dust well before you reach the doorway. Under the dark roof beams the sacks rise up in uneven walls, and the warmth coming off them lifts a haze that blurs and thickens the air. Because nobody ever thought to ventilate the place, the handlers swing the doors wide at daybreak, which draws in a flock of gray birds that no one there manages to chase back out. The scales sit in the middle, heavy, polished smooth by hands, and since they never rest, their pans have worn into a bright shallow bowl. The brick floor, ground down under the hand trucks, has split in a star beneath every pillar, so the carts jolt and the overflow from loosely tied sacks spills out in pale trails. Nobody bothers to sweep here. Everyone knows the dust will be back before dark.

units: grading a help desk by the number of calls handled is a mistake of method
the measure appeals because it is easy to work out
it turns harmful as soon as it sets what the teams are paid
an employee judged on speed cuts short the awkward exchanges
he passes the files on or closes requests he has settled badly
the quantity rises while satisfaction falls
the cost shifts onto the fresh calls from the same customers
it is proposed to weight the pace by the share of problems settled at once
an outside check ought to confirm that share
part of the work escapes any measure and belongs to the judgment of supervisors
text: Judging a help desk by the number of calls it handles is a mistake of method, and an expensive one at that. The measure appeals because it costs nothing to work out. It turns harmful the moment it sets what the teams take home. An adviser graded on speed learns fast to cut short the awkward conversations, to push the file over to another department, to close a request he knows was settled badly. Volume climbs, satisfaction falls away, and the real cost moves to the calls those same customers make again. There is a way out, though it takes nerve. Weight the pace against the share of cases resolved at first contact, and have an outside audit confirm that share. It also means owning that part of this work resists measurement, and leaving that part to the judgment of supervisors.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman now running a depot comes from the field of purchasing
her predecessor had been trained on the workshop floor
he judged performance by the quantity shipped
she judges performance by how stock moves and whether deadlines hold
the former manager settled tensions by talking and by his own standing
she prefers written rules put up for all to see and the same for everyone
he allowed private arrangements while she bargains for gains that cover all
the two ways of managing gave comparable financial results
the mood of the place changed between the two spells of leadership
text: The woman now running a materials depot took the job after a long career in purchasing. Her predecessor had come up from the workshop floor. He knew the machines, the movements, the tiredness of the crews, and he judged a week by what had gone out through the loading bay. She, trained in trade, looks first at how fast the stock turns over and at whether the delivery dates hold. The former manager settled trouble by talking and by the weight of his own standing. She prefers rules that are written, posted up, and the same for everyone. Where he allowed private arrangements, she bargains for gains the whole crew shares. The two methods brought in much the same margin, but not the same mood. Under him, people stayed late and nobody counted. Under her, they leave on time and talk more.

units: a retraining scheme meant for workers is judged uneven
the guidance stage is valued for its searching interviews
those interviews are led by people who come from the trade
they end in a written plan and not in a list of options
the equipment of the technical training is old and poorly suited
the machines of the employers differ from those used in training
the administrative help works well because compensation claims are dealt with on site
the follow-up after hiring stops too soon
most people who drop out do so after the opening stage of the contract
the yearly budget rules out any lasting planning
text: The retraining scheme offered to workers in an industrial area deserves a mixed verdict, since its parts differ so widely in quality. The guidance stage is strong. The interviews run long, they are led by people who have worked the trade themselves, and they end in a written plan rather than a list of possible paths. The technical training suffers from aging equipment, inherited from the shops that closed, which prepares people badly for the machines employers actually run. The administrative help convinces more, as the compensation claims are handled on site. Follow-up after hiring, by contrast, stops far too soon, when most of those who give up do so once the opening stretch of the contract is over. Funding, finally, hangs on yearly budgets, which rules out any lasting planning.
